notes.1ai: It was rare to see a wrong answer for this part. Occasionally a candidate failed to simplify and left the answer as 8:12.
notes.1aii: This was also nearly always correct but some methods were much longer than necessary.
notes.1aiii: Candidates had little problem finding the percentage. A few found the percentage Daniella received.
notes.1b: Most candidates obtained 31.83 and scored all 3 marks. Some did leave it as 31.827 or rounded to 3 s.f. A few who did it year-by-year spoilt the answer by adding the second year interest of 0.927 to 30 rather than 30.9. Only a very small number wrongly used simple interest.
notes.1c: This part was not answered as well. Some candidates confused interest and amount, using 32.25 as the interest. Some forgot to multiply by 100 and gave an answer of 0.015. Others tried to do a type of compound interest.
notes.2a: Very few candidates had a problem with this part, although some lost a mark by leaving the answer as 34 or 5.8 rather than 5.83. A few subtracted rather than added the two squares and obtained an answer of 4. 50 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2010
notes.2b: Most of the candidates correctly used the cosine rule and successfully obtained the correct answer. Occasional errors were seen with the use of the cosine rule and this normally occurred because 2 2 2 they started with the implicit version i.e. 11 = 8 + 5 – 2 × 5 × 8 cos ACD , and then, in rearranging, ended with 0.4 rather than -0.4. Some confused the angle required and found CAD instead. A few attempted to find the perpendicular from C to AD and then find the angle in two parts. Most made wrong assumptions in order to do this and earned no marks.
notes.2c: Good candidates normally scored full marks here and many others at least earned the method 1 1 marks by working out × 3 × 5 + × 8 × 5 × sin (their ACD ). There were also some attempts at 2 2 Hero’s formula, many of them correct.
notes.3a: This was almost always answered correctly even by weaker candidates.
notes.3b: Both parts of (b) were usually correct.
notes.3ci: Whilst many correctly obtained the correct answer, some multiplied 0.2 × 0.2 and gave an answer of 0.4. There were also some who used the method of “without replacement” in this part and also in the rest of part (c) and (d) , giving answers involving 9ths.
notes.3cii: Apart from those who used “without replacement”, most obtained the correct answer. Some only chose (1 and 3) and (2 and 2), missing out (3 and 1). Others chose (1 and 3) and (3 and 1) and (2 and 2) and (2 and 2). These answers did score 1 mark.
notes.3d: This was mostly correct except for those who used “without replacement”. A few tried a very long method of listing all the possible combinations. Usually they missed some out.
notes.4a: This part was well answered. Most candidates correctly reflected the triangle in y = 6, although a few reflected in x = 6 and even fewer in y = 0.
notes.4b: This part was also well answered, although there were more errors in this part. Most translated the triangle but some by the wrong amounts. The most common error was to translate 6 right and 4 down.
notes.4c: Most candidates described the translation correctly. Some gave the movement in words but the ⎛ − 4 ⎞ most common error was to give the vector as ⎜ ⎟ . ⎜ ⎟ ⎝ ⎠
notes.4di: Most candidates gave the transformation as enlargement, but marks were often lost by failing to give the centre or getting the scale factor wrong. Common wrong values were 2, -2 or – .
notes.4dii: Many correct but even some of the otherwise excellent candidates gave this answer as . 51 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2010
notes.4ei: This was the most testing part of the question. Shear rather than stretch was a common answer. There was again a problem with the scale factor with the same wrong answers as in part (d)(i) being quite common. Also many failed to state that the y -axis was invariant. It was quite common to say y invariant or parallel to the x -axis instead.
notes.5ai: This was mostly answered correctly. Wrong answers seen included congruent, same and proportional.
notes.5aii: This part was also mostly correct. Only a few mixed up the ratios and worked out 3.6 × . A few worked out 4 - 3.6 = 0.4 and then subtracted 0.4 from 3.
notes.5aiii: This part caused more problems. There were a lot of correct answers but some did a long method involving finding the angle ABC = AQP and then using × 3 × 2.7 × sin AQP to find the area. This method is of course correct and could earn full marks but many prematurely rounded and thus failed to obtain the exact answer of 3.15. A few failed to realise the need to square and calculated 5.6 × .
notes.5b: A lot of candidates obtained full marks in this part but some of the weaker candidates did not attempt it or only answered parts (i) and (ii) .
notes.5bi: Nearly all who attempted this part answered it correctly.
notes.5bii: This was also answered correctly by many but some gave an answer of 75.5 obtained by failing to recognise that TRH = 90 but instead treating triangle RHT as an isosceles triangle.
notes.5biv: Most candidates correctly subtracted the previous answer from 180 but some doubled their part
notes.5ci: Most gave the correct answer, although a few answered 4 or 24 .
notes.5cii: The more able candidates had little trouble with this part. However errors included using 360 or o o o 540 instead of 720 or obtaining an answer of 100 from 720/6 - 20. 52 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2010
notes.6c: This was not answered as well as the previous parts. Many stated k = 0 but failed to give the other two integer values.
notes.6a: Nearly everyone completed the table correctly.
notes.6b: The points were mostly correctly plotted and reasonable curves drawn. A few joined with straight lines and there were some who joined the two branches.
notes.6d: Most able candidates had no problem with this part but amongst the weaker candidates some did not attempt it, some included 0.5 or -0.5 in the inequalities, and some wrote the inequalities the wrong way round.
notes.6ei: The correct line y = 2 x +1 was usually drawn, although a few did not attempt this part.
notes.6eiii: Some of the weaker candidates failed to multiply through by x correctly and some failed to arrive at an equation of the form x + bx + c = 0. Those who did usually found the correct values for b and c .
notes.7a: Very few candidates confused mode, median and mean and most gave the correct value for all three. The most common error was to take the middle value as the 63rd rather than the 63.5th, so giving the median as 12 rather than 12.5.
notes.7bi: The histogram was interpreted very well with the majority finding the correct missing values. A few did make errors here and some did not attempt this part.
notes.7bii: The estimate of the mean was mostly calculated correctly by those who had found the values in the table. There were still a few who added the midpoints and divided by 6 but fewer made this error than previously.
notes.8a: Only a handful of candidates scored 2 marks in this part. The majority used a volume calculation thinking that this was equivalent to showing that 16 cuboids fit in the box. They did earn 1 mark.
notes.8ci: There were many different answers to this part. The majority did obtain 23640 but a variety of mistakes were made. The most common were failing to add 600 or not multiplying 180 by 8 and 16.
notes.8cii: Most correctly changed their answer in grams to kilograms. 53 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2010
notes.8di: A lot of good answers were seen here but a significant number failed to add together the correct areas. 156 from 4 × 10 × 3 + 2 × 6 × 3 was very common.
notes.8dii: Most candidates earned a mark for multiplying the previous answer by 16 and 25 but failed to 2 2 change correctly from cm to m . Some divided by 100 and a few did not seem to realise they needed to change the units.
notes.8e: Many candidates used the correct method for this part but often lost accuracy marks by premature approximation. They often rounded 104.7 to 105 and then subtracted from 180 giving an answer of 75 rather than 75.3. There were also a few who tried to subtract from 216 rather than 180.
notes.8f: This part proved difficult and only the stronger candidates scored well. Failing to divide by 20 at the start was quite common and many also failed to show their working. This did not matter if they arrived at the correct answer of 0.842 (or better). However if an answer of 0.84 appeared without working there was no way to tell if they had done the correct calculation. This meant that they would not get the marks for this part.
notes.9a: This part was well answered. Most candidates were able to set up the equations and the majority managed to solve them. A few made errors when eliminating one variable either by not multiplying every term by the same amount or by subtracting wrongly. A few tried trial and improvement rather than using simultaneous equations. If this resulted in the correct answers then they scored the marks but if the answers were wrong they earned zero.
notes.9bi: Good candidates had no problem with this part, showing sound ability to set up and manipulate algebraic equations. For the less able this caused all sorts of difficulties, not least not knowing how to find the time given distance and speed. Quite a large number made little or no attempt at this part.
notes.9bii: Most candidates factorised this correctly but a common wrong answer was y ( y – 13) + 12.
notes.9biii: Those who factorised correctly usually answered this correctly. A few others started again and used the formula to solve the equation.
notes.9biv: This again was mostly correct. A few answers of 12 appeared and weaker candidates often did not answer this part.
notes.9c: This was very well answered, even by some weaker candidates. The most common error was to get the first sign wrong in the formula and thus the answers had wrong signs.
notes.10a: Surprisingly, some excellent candidates missed this part. Practically everyone who attempted it did so correctly.
notes.10b: Nearly all candidates filled in the first two columns of the table correctly. A few made a slip. In the third column, most candidates correctly answered n and 4 n , but slightly fewer correctly filled in the final space. A few did not attempt this column. 54 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2010
notes.10cii: Again, this part was nearly always correct.
notes.10ciii: In this part there were also many correct answers but a few candidates did a lot of working and never arrived at 12 and a few gave the answer as 11.
